Most teams wait too long to evaluate their LLM features. They're looking for the *right*
framework when a small, honest rubric would already tell them most of what they need.

## The loop

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A[Collect 30 real prompts] --> B[Generate answers]
  B --> C{Score with rubric}
  C -->|pass| D[Ship]
  C -->|fail| E[Change prompt or model]
  E --> B
```

## The rubric

Three criteria, each scored 0–2. Keep it boring, keep it consistent.

```{python}
import pandas as pd

scores = pd.DataFrame({
    "variant":  ["Baseline", "Baseline", "Baseline", "New prompt", "New prompt", "New prompt"],
    "criterion": ["Correct", "Grounded", "Concise"] * 2,
    "score":    [1.2, 0.9, 1.6, 1.7, 1.5, 1.4],
})
scores.pivot(index="criterion", columns="variant", values="score")
```

## What changed

```{python}
#| label: fig-rubric
#| fig-cap: "Average rubric score by criterion (0–2)."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

wide = scores.pivot(index="criterion", columns="variant", values="score")
ax = wide.plot.bar(rot=0, width=0.7)
ax.set_title("The new prompt wins on correctness and grounding")
ax.set_xlabel("")
ax.set_ylim(0, 2)
ax.legend(title="")
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Rule of thumb
If every change "wins", your rubric isn't sensitive enough. Add a harder prompt or two.
:::

> Evaluate early, evaluate small, evaluate often.
